title: Nutrition and human growth in North America and Europe: 18th–20th century

paragraphs.text: Around 1850, the average American adult male stood about 170 centimeters, and weighed about 66 kilos. During the 1980s, the typical male in his early thirties was about 178 centimeters, and weighed about 79 kilos.

The 18th century was a difficult period in North America. Settlers were hindered by their basic farming implements, and limited agricultural knowledge. Harsh weather reduced the harvesting season. The possibilities for conducting trade were limited, and the population was subjected to major fluctuations in food production due to climate shocks. As a result, the supply of food was, at times, barely enough to sustain the agricultural laborers who were producing it. The diet was mainly composed of grains and cereals at first. In addition to wool, what little livestock was available was used more for milk than meat. However, in spite of these hardships, native-born North American men were taller, and had longer life expectancies than their European counterparts. This was probably because there was less communication of disease in North America due to a lower population density.

At the beginning of the 19th century, there were two conflicting trends affecting nutrition in the US. On the positive side, previously unknown techniques for farming were introduced, and at the same time the frontier expanded westward, creating additional land. These changes resulted in a large increase in crop production. On the other hand, the population also increased during the same period, by 338 percent. Crop production could not keep pace with the food required by the expanding industrial centers. As a result, per capita crop yield decreased. This raised prices and contributed to the nutritional decline of the population in the first half of the century.

It is estimated that the average US adult male consumed about 2,900 calories daily in 1800, which was roughly 20 percent higher than the average Englishman’s intake at that time. However, the decline in the country’s ability to produce cereals and meat at levels that would keep pace with population growth contributed to a net decrease in available food, and by 1850 daily intake was 2,585 calories per adult male. But food production started to increase again at the conclusion of the American Civil War in 1865, and by 1880 the average diet had reached a level that would be maintained for a further century.

In continental Europe, the picture was mixed. For example, the average height of French soldiers appears to have increased gradually over the 19th century, while the opposite was true for Dutch soldiers during this period. Moreover, there was a connection between height and social status. For example, between 1819 and 1826 students at an elite French school for military officers were 4 centimeters taller than ordinary men who were made to join the French national army. Also the more wealthy ordinary soldiers were taller than the poorer ones. Similar patterns have been observed in both the Netherlands and Spain.

Most scholars are in agreement that in Britain there was a general decline in the heights of both men and women between 1820 and 1850. Estimates put the extent of the decline at around 4.8 centimeters. Average heights began to rise once again after 1850, but even men who were born at the end of the 19th century were short by more recent standards, about six centimeters shorter than British men in the 1980s.

During the first half of the nineteenth century, a large proportion of the British population migrated from the countryside, and by 1850 more than half lived in urban areas. At this time Britain probably began to import more agricultural produce overall than it exported. The most dramatic change was in sugar, where imports increased by 150 percent between 1700 and 1850. Some scholars have suggested that domestic food production fell during this period, but there is evidence that it stayed constant while the number of calories obtained from imported foods increased. Still, it is possible that a significant proportion of the British population had diets below levels necessary to maintain weight. Furthermore, there is evidence that households compensated for a lack of calories by distributing a greater proportion of food to adult male workers, which may have contributed to the under-nutrition of children and women.

In conclusion, despite periodic fluctuations and regional differences in average body size over the last three hundred years of the previous millennium, the broad trend has been a considerable increase.
